entries.da6eea068406929bf1bf42facc7b33537d427927: <div sID="gen10564" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="14" osisID="Ps.14" sID="Ps.14"/> <div eID="gen10564" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10565" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen10566" type="x-p"/> It does not appear upon what occasion this psalm was penned nor whether upon any particular occasion. Some say David penned it when Saul persecuted him; others, when Absalom rebelled against him. But they are mere conjectures, which have not certainty enough to warrant us to expound the psalm by them. The apostle, in quoting part of this psalm (<reference osisRef="Rom.3.10">Rom. iii. 10</reference>, &c.) to prove that Jews and Gentiles are all under sin (<reference osisRef="Rom.3.9">ver. 9</reference>) and that all the world is guilty before God (<reference osisRef="Rom.3.19">ver. 19</reference>), leads us to understand it, in general, as a description of the depravity of human nature, the sinfulness of the sin we are conceived and born in, and the deplorable corruption of a great part of mankind, even of the world that lies in wickedness, <reference osisRef="1John.5.19">1 John v. 19</reference>. But as in those psalms which are designed to discover our remedy in Christ there is commonly an allusion to David himself, yea, and some passages that are to be understood primarily of him (as in <reference osisRef="Ps.2.1-Ps.2.12">psalm ii.</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.16.1-Ps.16.11">xvi,</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.22.1-Ps.22.31">xxii.</reference>, and others), so in this psalm, which is designed to discover our wound by sin, there is an allusion to David's enemies and persecutors, and other oppressors of good men at that time, to whom some passages have an immediate reference. In all the psalms from the 3rd to this (except the 8th) David had been complaining of those that hated and persecuted him, insulted him and abused him; now here he traces all those bitter streams to the fountain, the general corruption of nature, and sees that not his enemies only, but all the children of men, were thus corrupted. Here is, I. A charge exhibited against a wicked world, <reference osisRef="Ps.14.1">ver. 1</reference>. II. The proof of the charge, <reference osisRef="Ps.14.2-Ps.14.3">ver. 2, 3</reference>. III. A serious expostulation with sinners, especially with persecutors, upon it, <reference osisRef="Ps.14.4-Ps.14.6">ver. 4-6</reference>. IV. A believing prayer for the salvation of Israel and a joyful expectation of it, <reference osisRef="Ps.14.7">ver. 7</reference>.
entries.d7e5fba04b274433da431844260aab7aa9456f0a: <div eID="gen10566" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen10565" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Human Depravity.</title> <div sID="gen10567" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> The fool hath said in his heart, <hi type="italic">There is</hi> no God. They are corrupt, they have done abominable works, <hi type="italic">there is</hi> none that doeth good. <hi type="super">2</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> looked down from heaven upon the children of men, to see if there were any that did understand, <hi type="italic">and</hi> seek God. <hi type="super">3</hi> They are all gone aside, they are <hi type="italic">all</hi> together become filthy: <hi type="italic">there is</hi> none that doeth good, no, not one. <div eID="gen10567" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10568" type="x-p"/> If we apply our hearts as Solomon did (<reference osisRef="Eccl.7.25">Eccl. vii. 25</reference>) <hi type="italic">to search out the wickedness of folly, even of foolishness and madness,</hi> these verses will assist us in the search and will show us that sin is exceedingly sinful. Sin is the disease of mankind, and it appears here to be malignant and epidemic. <div eID="gen10568" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10569" type="x-p"/> 1. See how malignant it is (<reference osisRef="Ps.14.1">v. 1</reference>) in two things:— <div eID="gen10569" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10570" type="x-p"/> (1.) The contempt it puts upon the honour of God: for there is something of practical atheism at the bottom of all sin. <hi type="italic">The fool hath said in his heart, There is no God.</hi> We are sometimes tempted to think, "Surely there never was so much atheism and profaneness as there is in our days;" but we see the former days were no better; even in David's time there were those who had arrived at such a height of impiety as to deny the very being of a God and the first and self-evident principles of religion. Observe, [1.] The sinner here described. He is one that <hi type="italic">saith in his heart, There is no God;</hi> he is an atheist. "There is no <hi type="italic">Elohim,</hi> no Judge or governor of the world, no providence presiding over the affairs of men." They cannot doubt of the being of God, but will question his dominion. He says this <hi type="italic">in his heart;</hi> it is not his judgment, but his imagination. He cannot satisfy himself that there is none, but he wishes there were none, and pleases himself with the fancy that it is possible there may be none. He cannot be sure there is one, and therefore he is willing to think there is none. He dares not speak it out, lest he be confuted, and so undeceived, but he whispers it secretly <hi type="italic">in his heart,</hi> for the silencing of the clamours of his conscience and the emboldening of himself in his evil ways. [2.] The character of this sinner. He is a fool; he is simple and unwise, and this is an evidence of it; he is wicked and profane, and this is the cause of it. Note, Atheistical thoughts are very foolish wicked thoughts, and they are at the bottom of a great deal of the wickedness that is in this world. The word of God is a <hi type="italic">discerner of these thoughts,</hi> and puts a just brand on him that harbours them. <hi type="italic">Nabal is his name, and folly is with him;</hi> for he thinks against the clearest light, against his own knowledge and convictions, and the common sentiments of all the wise and sober part of mankind. No man will say, <hi type="italic">There is no God</hi> till he is so hardened in sin that it has become his interest that there should be none to call him to an account. <div eID="gen10570" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10571" type="x-p"/> (2.) The disgrace and debasement it puts upon the nature of man. Sinners are corrupt, quite degenerated from what man was in his innocent estate: <hi type="italic">They have become filthy</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.14.3">v. 3</reference>), putrid. All their faculties are so disordered that they have become odious to their Maker and utterly incapable of answering the ends of their creation. <hi type="italic">They are corrupt</hi> indeed; for, [1.] They do no good, but are the unprofitable burdens of the earth; they do God no service, bring him no honour, nor do themselves any real kindness. [2.] They do a great deal of hurt. <hi type="italic">They have done abominable works,</hi> for such all sinful works are. Sin is an abomination to God; it is that <hi type="italic">abominable thing which he hates</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.44.4">Jer. xliv. 4</reference>), and, sooner or later, it will be so to the sinner; it will be <hi type="italic">found to be hateful</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.36.2">Ps. xxxvi. 2</reference>), an <hi type="italic">abomination of desolation,</hi> that is, making desolate, <reference osisRef="Matt.24.15">Matt. xxiv. 15</reference>. This follows upon their saying, <hi type="italic">There is no God;</hi> for those that <hi type="italic">profess they know God, but in works deny him, are abominable, and to every good work reprobate,</hi> <reference osisRef="Titus.1.16">Tit. i. 16</reference>. <div eID="gen10571" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10572" type="x-p"/> 2. See how epidemic this disease is; it has infected the whole race of mankind. To prove this, God himself is here brought in for a witness, and he is an eye-witness, <reference osisRef="Ps.14.2-Ps.14.3">v. 2, 3</reference>. Observe, (1.) His enquiry: <hi type="italic">The Lord looked down from heaven,</hi> a place of prospect, which commands this lower world; thence, with an all-seeing eye, he took a view of all <hi type="italic">the children of men,</hi> and the question was, <hi type="italic">Whether there were any</hi> among them <hi type="italic">that did understand</hi> themselves aright, their duty and interests, and did seek God and set him before them. He that made this search was not only one that could find out a good man if he was to be found, though ever so obscure, but one that would be glad to find out one, and would be sure to take notice of him, as of Noah in the old world. (2.) The result of this enquiry, <reference osisRef="Ps.14.3">v. 3</reference>. Upon search, upon his search, it appeared, <hi type="italic">They have all gone aside,</hi> the apostasy is universal, <hi type="italic">there is none that doeth good, no, not one,</hi> till the free and mighty grace of God has wrought a change. Whatever good is in any of the children of men, or is done by them, it is not of themselves; it is God's work in them. When God had made the world he looked upon his own work, and <hi type="italic">all was very good</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.1.31">Gen. i. 31</reference>); but, some time after, he looked upon man's work, and, behold, all was very bad (<reference osisRef="Gen.6.5">Gen. vi. 5</reference>), every operation of the thought of man's heart was evil, only evil, and that continually. They have gone aside from the right of their duty, the way that leads to happiness, and have turned into the paths of the destroyer. <div eID="gen10572" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10573" type="x-p"/> In singing this let us lament the corruption of our own nature, and see what need we have of the grace of God; and, since that which is born of the flesh is flesh, let us not marvel that we are told we must be born again.
entries.1301f7e081e34dba115ff822b354caff38746f6f: <div eID="gen10573" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10574" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">4</hi> Have all the workers of iniquity no knowledge? who eat up my people <hi type="italic">as</hi> they eat bread, and call not upon the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">5</hi> There were they in great fear: for God <hi type="italic">is</hi> in the generation of the righteous. <hi type="super">6</hi> Ye have shamed the counsel of the poor, because the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">is</hi> his refuge. 7 Oh that the salvation of Israel <hi type="italic">were come</hi> out of Zion! when the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> bringeth back the captivity of his people, Jacob shall rejoice, <hi type="italic">and</hi> Israel shall be glad. <div eID="gen10574" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10575" type="x-p"/> In these verses the psalmist endeavours, <div eID="gen10575" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10576" type="x-p"/> I. To convince sinners of the evil and danger of the way they are in, how secure soever they are in that way. Three things he shows them, which, it may be, they are not very willing to see—their wickedness, their folly, and their danger, while they are apt to believe themselves very wise, and good, and safe. See here, <div eID="gen10576" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10577" type="x-p"/> 1. Their wickedness. This is described in four instances:—(1.) They are themselves <hi type="italic">workers of iniquity;</hi> they design it, they practise it, and take as much pleasure in it as ever any man did in his business. (2.) They <hi type="italic">eat up God's people</hi> with as much greediness <hi type="italic">as they eat bread,</hi> such an innate and inveterate enmity they have to them, and so heartily do they desire their ruin, because they really hate God, whose people they are. It is meat and drink to persecutors to be doing mischief; it is as agreeable to them as their necessary food. They eat up God's people easily, daily, securely, without either check of conscience when they do it or remorse of conscience when they have done it; as Joseph's brethren <hi type="italic">cast him into a pit</hi> and then <hi type="italic">sat down to eat bread,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.37.24-Gen.37.25">Gen. xxxvii. 24, 25</reference>. See <reference osisRef="Mic.3.2-Mic.3.3">Mic. iii. 2, 3</reference>. (3.) They <hi type="italic">call not upon the Lord.</hi> Note, Those that care not for God's people, for God's poor, care not for God himself, but live in contempt of him. The reason why people run into all manner of wickedness, even the worst, is because they do not call upon God for his grace. What good can be expected from those that live without prayer? (4.) They <hi type="italic">shame the counsel of the poor,</hi> and upbraid them with making God their refuge, as David's enemies upbraided him, <reference osisRef="Ps.11.1">Ps. xi. 1</reference>. Note, Those are very wicked indeed, and have a great deal to answer for, who not only shake off religion, and live without it themselves, but say and do what they can to put others out of conceit with it that are well-inclined—with the duties of it, as if they were mean, melancholy, and unprofitable, and with the privileges of it, as if they were insufficient to make a man safe and happy. Those that banter religion and religious people will find, to their cost, it is ill jesting with edged-tools and dangerous persecuting those that make God their refuge. <hi type="italic">Be you not mockers, lest your bands be made strong.</hi> He shows them, <div eID="gen10577" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10578" type="x-p"/> 2. Their folly: <hi type="italic">They have no knowledge;</hi> this is obvious, for if they had any knowledge of God, if they did rightly understand themselves, and would but consider things as men, they would not be so abusive and barbarous as they are to the people of God. <div eID="gen10578" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10579" type="x-p"/> 3. Their danger (<reference osisRef="Ps.14.5">v. 5</reference>): <hi type="italic">There were they in great fear.</hi> There, where they ate up God's people, their own consciences condemned what they did, and filled them with secret terrors; they sweetly sucked the blood of the saints, but in their bowels it is turned, and become the gall of asps. Many instances there have been of proud and cruel persecutors who have been made like Pashur, <hi type="italic">Magormissabibs—terrors to themselves</hi> and all about them. Those that will not fear God perhaps may be made to fear at the shaking of a leaf. <div eID="gen10579" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10580" type="x-p"/> II. He endeavours to comfort the people of God, 1. With what they have. They have God's presence (<reference osisRef="Ps.14.5">v. 5</reference>): He <hi type="italic">is in the generation of the righteous.</hi> They have his protection (<reference osisRef="Ps.14.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">The Lord is their refuge.</hi> This is as much their security as it is the terror of their enemies, who may jeer them for their confidence in God, but cannot jeer them out of it. In the judgment-day it will add to the terror and confusion of sinners to see God own the generation of the righteous, which they have hated and bantered. 2. With what they hope for; and that is the <hi type="italic">salvation of Israel,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.14.7">v. 7</reference>. When David was driven out by Absalom and his rebellious accomplices, he comforted himself with an assurance that god would in due time <hi type="italic">turn again his captivity,</hi> to the joy of all his good subjects. But surely this pleasing prospect looks further. He had, in the beginning of the psalm, lamented the general corruption of mankind; and, in the melancholy view of that, wishes for the salvation which should be wrought out by the Redeemer, who was expected <hi type="italic">to come to Zion,</hi> to <hi type="italic">turn away ungodliness from Jacob,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.11.26">Rom. xi. 26</reference>. The world is bad; O that the Messiah would come and change its character! There is a universal corruption; O for the times of reformation! Those will be as joyful times as these are melancholy ones. Then shall God <hi type="italic">turn again the captivity of his people;</hi> for the Redeemer shall <hi type="italic">ascend on high, and lead captivity captive,</hi> and Jacob shall then rejoice. The triumphs of Zion's King will be the joys of Zion's children. The second coming of Christ, finally to extinguish the dominion of sin and Satan, will be the completing of this salvation, which is the hope, and will be the joy, of every Israelite indeed. With the assurance of that we should, in singing this, comfort ourselves and one another, with reference to the present sins of sinners and sufferings of saints.  <chapter eID="Ps.14"/> <div eID="gen10580" type="x-p"/>

entries.1b7e646d5bd51266b42fe8428b68322e81d8356e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5578"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 14</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.14.1-Ps.14.7">Psa 14:1-7</reference>. The practical atheism and total and universal depravity of the wicked, with their hatred to the good, are set forth. Yet, as they dread God's judgments when He vindicates His people, the Psalmist prays for His delivering power.</title> <div sID="gen8466" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5578"/>1. Sinners are termed "fools," because they think and act contrary to right reason (<reference osisRef="Gen.34.7">Ge 34:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.7.15">Jos 7:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.39.8">Psa 39:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.74.18">74:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.74.22">22</reference>).<div eID="gen8466" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8467" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in his heart--</hi>to himself (<reference osisRef="Gen.6.12">Ge 6:12</reference>). <div eID="gen8467" type="x-p"/>
entries.91eaa8916f33953ee6ca1d9374b23d35611733bf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5579"/><div sID="gen8468" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5579"/><hi type="bold">2. looked--</hi>in earnest enquiry.<div eID="gen8468" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8469" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">understand--</hi>as opposed to "fool" [Psa 14:1]. <div eID="gen8469" type="x-p"/>
entries.769ea9bb2feff6de0d46b8c585d02cc60af5b722: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5580"/><div sID="gen8470" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5580"/><hi type="bold">3. filthy--</hi>literally, "spoiled," or, "soured," "corrupted" (<reference osisRef="Job.15.16">Job 15:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.3.12">Ro 3:12</reference>). <div eID="gen8470" type="x-p"/>
entries.daed8378ca302fe7c63aaf381ef33d7b1a004c7f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5581"/><div sID="gen8471" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5581"/>4-6. Their conduct evinces indifference rather than ignorance of God; for when He appears in judgment, they are stricken with great fear.<div eID="gen8471" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8472" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">who eat up my people--</hi>to express their beastly fury (<reference osisRef="Prov.30.14">Pr 30:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hab.3.14">Ha 3:14</reference>). To "call on the Lord" is to worship Him. <div eID="gen8472" type="x-p"/>
entries.7017df3d78452c0c0e728680432e0dfe71f84311: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5582"/><div sID="gen8473" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5582"/><hi type="bold">7. captivity--</hi>denotes any great evil.<div eID="gen8473" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8474" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Zion--</hi>God's abode, from which He revealed His purposes of mercy, as He now does by the Church (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.3.4">Psa 3:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.20.2">20:2</reference>), and which He rules and in which He does all other things for the good of His people (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.22">Ep 1:22</reference>). <chapter eID="Ps.14"/>

entries.50a9bae4a2b97695ff10912670e33208b4d66c0c: <div eID="gen18715" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen18716" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen18717" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen18717" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen18716" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen18718" type="x-p"/> The sentiments of atheists and deists, who deny the doctrine of a Divine providence. Their character: they are corrupt, foolish, abominable, and cruel, <reference osisRef="Psa.14.1-Psa.14.4">Psa 14:1-4</reference>. God fills them with terror, <reference osisRef="Psa.14.5">Psa 14:5</reference>; reproaches them for their oppression of the poor, <reference osisRef="Psa.14.6">Psa 14:6</reference>. The psalmist prays for the restoration of Israel, <reference osisRef="Psa.14.7">Psa 14:7</reference>. <div eID="gen18718" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18719" type="x-p"/> There is nothing particular in the title; only it is probable that the word לדוד ledavid, of David, is improperly prefixed, as it is sufficiently evident, from the construction of the Psalm, that it speaks of the Babylonish captivity. The author, whoever he was, (some say Haggai, others Daniel, etc)., probably lived beyond the Euphrates. He describes here, in fervid colors, the iniquity of the Chaldeans. He predicts their terror and destruction; he consoles himself with the prospect of a speedy return from his exile; and hopes soon to witness the reunion of the tribes of Israel and Judah. It may be applied to unbelievers in general. <div eID="gen18719" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18720" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen18720" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18721" type="x-p"/> The fool hath said in his heart, There is no God - נבל nabal, which we render fool, signifies an empty fellow, a contemptible person, a villain. One who has a muddy head and an unclean heart; and, in his darkness and folly, says in his heart, "There is no God." "And none," says one, "but a fool would say so." The word is not to be taken in the strict sense in which we use the term atheist, that is, one who denies the being of a God, or confounds him with matter. 1. There have been some, not many, who have denied the existence of God. 2. There are others who, without absolutely denying the Divine existence, deny his providence; that is, they acknowledge a Being of infinite power, etc., but give him nothing to do, and no world to govern. 3. There are others, and they are very numerous, who, while they profess to acknowledge both, deny them in their heart, and live as if they were persuaded there was no God either to punish or reward. <div eID="gen18721" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18722" type="x-p"/> They are corrupt - They are in a state of putrescence and they have done abominable works - the corruption of their hearts extends itself through all the actions of their lives. They are a plague of the most deadly kind; propagate nothing but destruction; and, like their father the devil, spread far and wide the contagion of sin and death. Not one of them does good. He cannot, for he has no Divine influence, and he denies that such can be received.
entries.4b91c6d1bde00715a181d1af1da9290821cba869: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen18722" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18723" type="x-p"/> The Lord looked down from heaven - Words spoken after the manner of men. From this glorious eminence God is represented as looking down upon the habitable globe, to see if there were any that did understand that there was a Supreme Being, the governor and judge of men; and, in consequence, seek God for his mercy, support, and defense.
entries.08ef1c580e1607e50661fb64a6acfb99e00079d8: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen18723" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18724" type="x-p"/> They are all gone aside - They will not walk in the straight path. They seek crooked ways; and they have departed from truth, and the God of truth. <div eID="gen18724" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18725" type="x-p"/> They are all together become filthy - נאלחו neelachu. They are become sour and rancid; a metaphor taken from milk that has fermented and turned sour, rancid, and worthless. <div eID="gen18725" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18726" type="x-p"/> There is none that doeth good, no, not one - This is not only the state of heathen Babylon! but the state of the whole inhabitants of the earth, till the grace of God changes their heart. By nature, and from nature, by practice, every man is sinful and corrupt. He feels no good; he is disposed to no good; he does no good. And even God himself, who cannot be deceived, cannot find a single exception to this! Lord, what is man? <div eID="gen18726" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18727" type="x-p"/> The Vulgate, the Roman copy of the Septuagint, the Athtopic, and the Arabic, add those six verses here which are quoted by St. Paul, <reference osisRef="Rom.3.13-Rom.3.18">Rom 3:13-18</reference> (note). See the observations at the end of this Psalm.
entries.8df64858093b0adf18c721bef0ece53151da90c0: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen18727" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18728" type="x-p"/> Have all the workers of iniquity no knowledge? - Is there not one of them who takes this dreadful subject into consideration? To their deeply fallen state they add cruelty; they oppress and destroy the poor, without either interest or reason. <div eID="gen18728" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18729" type="x-p"/> Who eat up my people as they eat bread - Ye make them an easy and unresisting prey. They have no power to oppose you, and therefore you destroy them. That this is the meaning of the expression, is plain from the speech of Joshua and Caleb relative to the Canaanites. <reference osisRef="Num.14.9">Num 14:9</reference> : "Neither fear ye the people or the land; for they are bread for us." <div eID="gen18729" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18730" type="x-p"/> And call not upon the Lord - They have no defense, for they invoke not the Lord. They are all either atheists or idolaters.
entries.62a3b1c847219865a80607d549173e5ffd55b2d4: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen18730" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18731" type="x-p"/> There were they in great fear - This is a manifest allusion to the history of the Canaanitish nations; they were struck with terror at the sight of the Israelites, and by this allusion the psalmist shows that a destruction similar to that which fell upon them, should fall on the Babylonians. Several of the versions add, from <reference osisRef="Psa.53.5">Psa 53:5</reference>, "Where no fear was." They were struck with terror, where no real cause of terror existed. Their fears had magnified their danger. <div eID="gen18731" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18732" type="x-p"/> For God is in the generation - They feared the Israelites, because they knew that the Almighty God was among them.
entries.c1002a5f826b4ea7b1b3cba5e27fae28e30a00fd: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen18732" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18733" type="x-p"/> Ye have shamed the counsel of the poor - Instead of תבישו tabishu, "Ye have shamed," Bishop Horsley proposes to read תבישם tabishem, and translates the clause thus: "The counsel of the helpless man shall put them to shame." But this is not authorized by MS. or version. There is no need for any change: the psalmist refers to the confidence which the afflicted people professed to have in God for their deliverance, which confidence the Babylonians turned into ridicule. The poor people took counsel together to expect help from God and to wait patiently for it; and this counsel ye derided, because ye did not know - did not consider, that God was in the congregation of the righteous.
entries.120b6058d0db642cf78103f2ac5f378357600700: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen18733" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18734" type="x-p"/> O that the salvation - Or, more literally, Who will give from Zion salvation to Israel? From Zion the deliverance must come; for God alone can deliver them; but whom will he make his instruments? <div eID="gen18734" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18735" type="x-p"/> When the Lord bringeth back - For it is Jehovah alone who can do it. Jacob shall rejoice and Israel shall be glad. That is, according to Calmet, the remains of the kingdom of Israel and those of Judah, shall be rejoined, to their mutual satisfaction, and become one people, worshipping the same God; and he has endeavoured to prove, in a dissertation on the subject, that this actually took place after the return from the Babylonish captivity. <div eID="gen18735" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18736" type="x-p"/> Many of the fathers have understood this verse as referring to the salvation of mankind by Jesus Christ; and so it is understood by my old MS. Psalter, as the following paraphrase will show: Qwa sal gyf of Syon hele til Israel? qwen Lord has turned a way the captyfte of his folk, glad sal Jacob, and fayne be Israel. Qwa bot Crist that ge despyse, qwen ge wit nout do his counsaile of Syon fra heven, sal gyf hele til Israel? that es, sal saf al trew cristen men, noght als ge er that lufs noght God. And qwen our Lord has turned o way the captyfte of his folk: that es, qwen he has dampned the devel, and al his Servaundes, the qwilk tourmentes gude men, and makes tham captyfs in pyne. Then glade sal Jacob; that es, al that wirstils o gayns vices and actyf: and fayne sal be Israel: that es, al that with the clene egh of thair hert, sees God in contemplatyf lyf. For Jacob es als mikil at say als, Wrestler, or suplanter of Syn. Israel es, man seand God. <div eID="gen18736" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18737" type="x-p"/> Of the two chief opinions relative to the design of this Psalm: <div eID="gen18737" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18738" type="x-p"/> 1. That it refers to Absalom's rebellion. <div eID="gen18738" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18739" type="x-p"/> 2. That it is a complaint of the captives in Babylon; I incline to the latter, as by far the most probable. <div eID="gen18739" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18740" type="x-p"/> I have referred, in the note on <reference osisRef="Psa.14.3">Psa 14:3</reference>, to that remarkable addition of no less than six verses, which is found here in the Vulgate, the Vatican copy of the Septuagint, the Ethiopic, and the Arabic, and also in St. Paul's Epistle to the Romans, <reference osisRef="Rom.3.13-Rom.3.18">Rom 3:13-18</reference>, which he is supposed to have quoted from this Psalm as it then stood in the Hebrew text; or in the version of the Seventy, from which it has been generally thought he borrowed them. That they are not interpolations in the New Testament is evident from this, that they are not wanting in any MS. yet discovered; and they exist in all the ancient versions, the Vulgate, Syriac, Ethiopic, and Arabic. Yet it has been contended, particularly by St. Jerome, that St. Paul did not quote them from this Psalm; but, being intent on showing the corruption and misery of man, he collected from different parts several passages that bore upon the subject, and united them here, with his quotation from <reference osisRef="Psa.14.3">Psa 14:3</reference>, as if they had all belonged to that place: and that succeeding copyists, finding them in Romans, as quoted from that Psalm, inserted them into the Septuagint, from which it was presumed they had been lost. It does not appear that they made a part of this Psalm in Origen's Hexapla. In the portions that still exist of this Psalm there is not a word of these additional verses referred to in that collection, neither here nor in the parallel <reference osisRef="Psa.53.1-Psa.53.6">Psa 53:1-6</reference>. <div eID="gen18740" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18741" type="x-p"/> The places from which Jerome and others say St. Paul borrowed them are the following: - <reference osisRef="Rom.3.13">Rom 3:13</reference> : "Their mouth is an open sepulchre; with their tongues they have used deceit." Borrowed from <reference osisRef="Psa.5.10">Psa 5:10</reference>. "The poison of asps is under their lips." From <reference osisRef="Psa.140.3">Psa 140:3</reference>. <reference osisRef="Rom.3.14">Rom 3:14</reference> : "Whose mouth is full of cursing and bitterness." From <reference osisRef="Psa.10.7">Psa 10:7</reference>. <reference osisRef="Rom.3.15">Rom 3:15</reference> : "Their feet are swift to shed blood." From <reference osisRef="Pro.1.16">Pro 1:16</reference>, or <reference osisRef="Isa.59.7">Isa 59:7</reference>. <reference osisRef="Rom.3.16-Rom.3.18">Rom 3:16-18</reference> : "Destruction and misery are in their ways, the way of peace they have not known, and there is no fear of God before their eyes." From <reference osisRef="Isa.59.7">Isa 59:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.59.8">Isa 59:8</reference>. <div eID="gen18741" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18742" type="x-p"/> When the reader has collated all these passages in the original, he will probably feel little satisfaction relative to the probability of the hypothesis they are summoned to support. <div eID="gen18742" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18743" type="x-p"/> These verses are not found in the best copies of the Vulgate, though it appears they were in the old Itala or Antehieronymain version. They are not in the Codex Alexandrinus of the Septuagint; nor are they in either the Greek or Latin text of the Complutenstan Polyglot. They are wanting also in the Antwerp and Parisian Polyglots. They are neither in the Chaldee nor Syriac versions. They are not acknowledged as a part of this Psalm by Theodoret, Chrysostom, Euthymius, Arnobius, Apollinaris, the Greek Catena, Eusebius, of Caesarea, nor Jerome. The latter, however, acknowledges that they were in his time read in the churches. I have seen no Latin MS. without them; and they are quoted by Justin Martyr and Augustine. They are also in the Editio Princeps of the Vulgate, and in all the ancient Psalters known. They are in that Psalter which I have frequently quoted, both in the Latino - Scotico - English version and paraphrase. <div eID="gen18743" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18744" type="x-p"/> Of this version the following is a faithful copy, beginning with the third verse of the fourteenth Psalm: - <div eID="gen18744" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18745" type="x-p"/> Al tha helddid togyher; thai er made unprofytable: <div eID="gen18745" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18746" type="x-p"/> Thar es none that dos gude; thar es none til one. <div eID="gen18746" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18747" type="x-p"/> A grave opynnand, es the throte of tham. <div eID="gen18747" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18748" type="x-p"/> With thaire tunges trycherusly thai wroght <div eID="gen18748" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18749" type="x-p"/> Venym of snakes undir the lippis of tham. <div eID="gen18749" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18750" type="x-p"/> Qwhas mouth es ful of werying and bitternes: <div eID="gen18750" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18751" type="x-p"/> Swyft thaire fete to spil blode. <div eID="gen18751" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18752" type="x-p"/> Brekyng and wikednes in thair waies: <div eID="gen18752" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18753" type="x-p"/> And the way of pees thai knew noght: <div eID="gen18753" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18754" type="x-p"/> The drede of God es noght byfore the eghen of thaim. <div eID="gen18754" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18755" type="x-p"/> There is a good deal of difference between this, and that version attributed to Wiclif, as it stands in my large MS. Bible, quoted in different parts of the New Testament, particularly in <reference osisRef="1Cor.13.1">1Cor 13:1</reference>, etc. I shall give it here line for line with the above. <div eID="gen18755" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18756" type="x-p"/> Alle boweden aweye to gydre: thei ben maad unprofitable: <div eID="gen18756" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18757" type="x-p"/> There is not that doith good thing, ther is not to oon. <div eID="gen18757" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18758" type="x-p"/> A Sepulcre opnyng is the throote of hem: <div eID="gen18758" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18759" type="x-p"/> With her tungis thei diden gylinly; or trecherously: <div eID="gen18759" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18760" type="x-p"/> The venym of eddris, that is clepid Aspis, under her lippis: <div eID="gen18760" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18761" type="x-p"/> The mouth of whom is ful of cursing, or worrying and bittrenesse: <div eID="gen18761" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18762" type="x-p"/> The feet of hem ben swift to schede out blood: <div eID="gen18762" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18763" type="x-p"/> Contricion or defouling to God, and infelicite or cursidnesse, the wayes of hem; <div eID="gen18763" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18764" type="x-p"/> And thei knewen not the weyes of pees; <div eID="gen18764" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18765" type="x-p"/> The dreed of God is not bifore her ygen. <div eID="gen18765" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18766" type="x-p"/> The words underlined in the above are added by the translator as explanatory of the preceding terms. It is worthy of remark that Coverdale inserts the whole of the addition in this Psalm, and Cardmarden has inserted it in his Bible, but in a letter different from the text. <div eID="gen18766" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18767" type="x-p"/> It is now time to state what has been deemed of considerable importance to the authenticity of these verses; viz., that they are found in a Hebrew MS., numbered by Kennicott in his catalogue 649. It is in the public library at Leyden; contains the Psalms with a Latin version and Scholia; and appears to have been written about the end of the fourteenth century and probably by some Christian. I shall give the text with a literal translation, as it stands in this MS., line for line with the preceding: - קבר פתוח גרונם <div eID="gen18767" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18768" type="x-p"/> An open sepulcher is their throat; לשונם יחליקיו <div eID="gen18768" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18769" type="x-p"/> With their tongues they flatter; חמת עכשוב תחת לשונם <div eID="gen18769" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18770" type="x-p"/> The venom of the asp is under their tongue; אשר פיהם אלה ומרמה מלא <div eID="gen18770" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18771" type="x-p"/> Whose mouth of cursing and bitterness is full; קלו רגליהם לשפוך דם <div eID="gen18771" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18772" type="x-p"/> Swift are their feet to shed blood; מזל רע ופגע רע בדרכיהם <div eID="gen18772" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18773" type="x-p"/> An evil aspect, and an evil event, in their ways: ודרך שלום לא ידעו <div eID="gen18773" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18774" type="x-p"/> And the way of peace they know not. אי פחד אלהים לנגר עיניהם <div eID="gen18774" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18775" type="x-p"/> No fear of God before their eyes. <div eID="gen18775" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18776" type="x-p"/> It would be easy to criticise upon the Hebrew In this long quotation. I shall content myself with what Calmet, who received his information from others that had inspected the Leyden MS., says of this addition: "Les seavans, qui ont examine ce manuscrit, y ont remarque un Hebreu barbare en cet endroit; et des facons de parler, qui ne sentent point les siecles ou la langue Hebraique etoit en usage." "Learned men, who have examined this MS., have remarked a barbarous Hebraism in this place, and modes of speech which savor not of those ages in which the Hebrew language was in use." <div eID="gen18776" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18777" type="x-p"/> If this be an interpolation in the Psalm, it is very ancient; as we have the testimony of Jerome, who was prejudiced against it, that it was read in all the churches in his time, and how long before we cannot tell. And that these verses are a valuable portion of Divine revelation, as they stand in <reference osisRef="Rom.3.13-Rom.3.18">Rom 3:13-18</reference>, none can successfully deny. See Rosenmuller, Kennicott, and De Rossi.  <chapter eID="Ps.14"/> <div eID="gen18777" type="x-p"/>

entries.34a9a7fb63b2c9cbdfab70aabe5566a608cc77e4: <div eID="gen9149" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">The Prevailing Corruption and the Redemption Desired</title> <div sID="gen9150" type="x-p"/> Just as the general lamentation of <reference osisRef="Ps.12.1-Ps.12.8">Psa 12:1-8</reference> assumes a personal character in <reference osisRef="Ps.13.1-Ps.13.6">Psa 13:1-6</reference>, so in <reference osisRef="Ps.14.1-Ps.14.7">Psa 14:1-7</reference> it becomes again general; and the personal desire יגל לבּי, <reference osisRef="Ps.13.5">Psa 13:5</reference>, so full of hope, corresponds to יגל יעקב, which is extended to the whole people of God in Psa 14:7. Moreover, <reference osisRef="Ps.14.1-Ps.14.7">Psa 14:1-7</reference>, as being a gloomy picture of the times in which the dawn of the divine day is discernible in the background, is more closely allied to <reference osisRef="Ps.12.1-Ps.12.8">Psa 12:1-8</reference> than to <reference osisRef="Ps.13.1-Ps.13.6">Psa 13:1-6</reference>, although this latter is not inserted between them without some recognised reason. In the reprobation of the moral and religious character of the men of the age, which <reference osisRef="Ps.14.1-Ps.14.7">Psa 14:1-7</reference> has in common with <reference osisRef="Ps.12.1-Ps.12.8">Psa 12:1-8</reference>, we at once have a confirmation of the לדוד. But <reference osisRef="Ps.14.7">Psa 14:7</reference> does not necessitate our coming down to the time of the Exile. <div eID="gen9150" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9151" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="Ps.53.1-Ps.53.6">Psa 53:1-6</reference> we find this Psalm which is Jehovic, occurring again as Elohimic. The position of <reference osisRef="Ps.14.1-Ps.14.7">Psa 14:1-7</reference> in the primary collection favours the presumption, that it is the earlier and more original composition. And since this presumption will bear the test of a critical comparison of the two Psalms, we may leave the treatment of <reference osisRef="Ps.53.1-Ps.53.6">Psa 53:1-6</reference> to its proper place, without bringing it forward here. It is not as though <reference osisRef="Ps.14.1-Ps.14.7">Psa 14:1-7</reference> were intact. It is marked out as seven three-line verses, but <reference osisRef="Ps.14.5">Psa 14:5</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ps.14.6">Psa 14:6</reference>, which ought to be the fifth and sixth three lines, are only two; and the original form appears to be destroyed by some deficiency. The difficulty is got over in <reference osisRef="Ps.53.1-Ps.53.6">Psa 53:1-6</reference>, by making the two two-line verses into one three-line verse, so that it consists only of six three-line verses. And in that Psalm the announcement of judgment is applied to foreign enemies, a circumstance which has influenced some critics and led them astray in the interpretation of <reference osisRef="Ps.14.1">Psa 14:1</reference>-7. <div eID="gen9151" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9152" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Ps.14.1">Psa 14:1</reference> <div eID="gen9152" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9153" type="x-p"/> The perfect אמר, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.1.1">Psa 1:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.10.3">Psa 10:3</reference>, is the so-called abstract present (Ges. §126, 3), expressing a fact of universal experience, inferred from a number of single instances. The Old Testament language is unusually rich in epithets for the unwise. The simple, פּתי, and the silly, כּסיל, for the lowest branches of this scale; the fool, אויל, and the madman, הולל, the uppermost. In the middle comes the notion of the simpleton or maniac, נבל - a word from the verbal stem נבל which, according as that which forms the centre of the group of consonants lies either in נב (<hi type="italic">Genesis</hi> S. 636), or in בל (comp. אבל, אול, אמל, קמל), signifies either to be extended, to relax, to become frail, to wither, or to be prominent, <hi type="italic">eminere</hi>, Arab. <hi type="italic">nabula</hi>; so that consequently נבל means the relaxed, powerless, expressed in New Testament language: πνεῦμα οὐκ ἔχοντα. Thus Isaiah (<reference osisRef="Isa.32.6">Isa 32:6</reference>) describes the נבל: “a simpleton speaks simpleness and his heart does godless things, to practice tricks and to say foolish things against Jahve, to leave the soul of the hungry empty, and to refuse drink to the thirsty.” Accordingly נבל is the synonym of לץ the scoffer (vid., the definition in <reference osisRef="Prov.21.24">Pro 21:24</reference>). A free spirit of this class is reckoned according to the Scriptures among the empty, hollow, and devoid of mind. The thought, אין אלהים, which is the root of the thought and action of such a man, is the climax of imbecility. It is not merely practical atheism, that is intended by this maxim of the נבל. The heart according to Scripture language is not only the seat of volition, but also of thought. The נבל is not content with acting as though there were no God, but directly denies that there is a God, i.e., a personal God. The psalmist makes this prominent as the very extreme and depth of human depravity, that there can be among men those who deny the existence of a God. The subject of what follows are, then, not these atheists but men in general, among whom such characters are to be found: they make the mode of action, (their) doings, corrupt, they make it abominable. עלילה, a poetical brevity of expression for עלילותם, belongs to both verbs, which have <hi type="italic">Tarcha</hi> and <hi type="italic">Mercha</hi> (the two usual conjunctives of <hi type="italic">Mugrash</hi>) in correct texts; and is in fact not used as an adverbial accusative (Hengstenberg and others), but as an object, since השׁהית is just the word that is generally used in this combination with עלילה Zep 3:7 or, what is the same thing, דּרך <reference osisRef="Gen.6.12">Gen 6:12</reference>; and התעיב (cf. 1Ki 21:26) is only added to give a superlative intensity to the expression. The negative: “there is none that doeth good” is just as unrestricted as in Psa 12:2. But further on the psalmist distinguishes between a דור צדיק, which experiences this corruption in the form of persecution, and the corrupt mass of mankind. He means what he says of mankind as κόσμος, in which, at first the few rescued by grace from the mass of corruption are lost sight of by him, just as in the words of God, <reference osisRef="Gen.6.5">Gen 6:5</reference>, Gen 6:12. Since it is only grace that frees any from the general corruption, it may also be said, that men are described just as they are by nature; although, be it admitted, it is not hereditary sin but actual sin, which springs up from it, and grows apace if grace do not interpose, that is here spoken of.
entries.ee3a17fdb627358a7d7d3479223ced8cd20a840f: <reference osisRef="Ps.14.2">Psa 14:2</reference> <div eID="gen9153" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9154" type="x-p"/> The second tristich appeals to the infallible decision of God Himself. The verb השׁקיף means to look forth, by bending one’s self forward. It is the proper word for looking out of a window, 2Ki 9:30 (cf. <hi type="italic">Niph</hi>. Jdg 5:28, and frequently), and for God’s looking down from heaven upon the earth, <reference osisRef="Ps.102.20">Psa 102:20</reference>, and frequently; and it is cognate and synonymous with השׁגּיח, <reference osisRef="Ps.33.13">Psa 33:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.33.14">Psa 33:14</reference>; cf. moreover, Sol 2:9. The <hi type="italic">perf</hi>. is used in the sense of the perfect only insofar as the divine survey is antecedent to its result as given in Psa 14:3. Just as השׁהיתוּ reminds one of the history of the Flood, so does לראות of the history of the building of the tower of Babel, <reference osisRef="Gen.11.5">Gen 11:5</reference>, cf. Psa 18:21. God’s judgment rests upon a knowledge of the matter of fact, which is represented in such passages after the manner of men. God’s all-seeing, all-piercing eyes scrutinise the whole human race. Is there one who shows discernment in thought and act, one to whom fellowship with God is the highest good, and consequently that after which he strives? - this is God’s question, and He delights in such persons, and certainly none such would escape His longing search. On את־אלהים, τὸν Θεόν, vid., Ges. §117, 2.
entries.c69fe1479376889df1739489184d69cfd9e7bdc3: <reference osisRef="Ps.14.3">Psa 14:3</reference> <div eID="gen9154" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9155" type="x-p"/> The third tristich bewails the condition in which He finds humanity. The universality of corruption is expressed in as strong terms as possible. הכּל they all (lit., the totality); יחדּו with one another (lit., in its or their unions, i.e., <hi type="italic">universi</hi>); אין גּם־אחד not a single one who might form an exception. סר (probably not <hi type="italic">3 praet</hi>. but <hi type="italic">partic</hi>., which passes at once into the finite verb) signifies to depart, viz., from the ways of God, therefore to fall away (ἀποστάτης). נאלח, as in <reference osisRef="Job.15.16">Job 15:16</reference>, denotes the moral corruptness as a becoming sour, putrefaction, and suppuration. Instead of אין גּם־אחד, the lxx translates οὐκ ἔστιν ἕως ἑνός (as though it were עד־אחד, which is the more familiar form of expression). Paul quotes the first three verses of this Psalm (<reference osisRef="Rom.3.10-Rom.3.12">Rom 3:10-12</reference>) in order to show how the assertion, that Jews and heathen all are included under sin, is in accordance with the teaching of Scripture. What the psalmist says, applies primarily to Israel, his immediate neighbours, but at the same time to the heathen, as is self-evident. What is lamented is neither the pseudo-Israelitish corruption in particular, nor that of the heathen, but the universal corruption of man which prevails not less in Israel than in the heathen world. The citations of the apostle which follow his quotation of the Psalm, from τάφος ἀνεῳγμένος to ἀπέναντι τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν αὐτῶν were early incorporated in the Psalm in the Κοινή of the lxx. They appear as an integral part of it in the <hi type="italic">Cod. Alex</hi>., in the Greco-Latin <hi type="italic">Psalterium Vernonense</hi>, and in the Syriac <hi type="italic">Psalterium Mediolanense</hi>. They are also found in Apollinaris’ paraphrase of the Psalms as a later interpolation; the <hi type="italic">Cod. Vat</hi>. has them in the margin; and the words σύντπιμμα καὶ ταλαιπωρία ἐν ταῖς ὁδοῖς αὐτῶν have found admittance in the translation, which is more Rabbinical than Old Hebrew, מזּל רע וּפגע רע בּדרכיהם even in a Hebrew codex (Kennicott 649). Origen rightly excluded this apostolic Mosaic work of Old Testament testimonies from his text of the Psalm; and the true representation of the matter is to be found in Jerome, in the preface to the xvi. book of his commentary on Isaiah.<note placement="foot">Cf. Plüschke’s Monograph on the Milanese <hi type="italic">Psalterium Syriacum</hi>, 1835, p. 28-39.</note>
entries.6f9d62ceb9a1eda32adcd865e626c8382650c167: <reference osisRef="Ps.14.4">Psa 14:4</reference> <div eID="gen9155" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9156" type="x-p"/> Thus utterly cheerless is the issue of the divine scrutiny. It ought at least to have been different in Israel, the nation of the positive revelation. But even there wickedness prevails and makes God’s purpose of mercy of none effect. The divine outburst of indignation which the psalmist hears here, is applicable to the sinners in Israel. Also in <reference osisRef="Isa.3.13-Isa.3.15">Isa 3:13-15</reference> the Judge of the world addresses Himself to the heads of Israel in particular. This one feature of the Psalm before us is raised to the consistency of a special prophetic picture in the Psalm of Asaph, <reference osisRef="Ps.82.1">Psa 82:1</reference>-8. That which is here clothed in the form of a question, הלא ידעוּ, is reversed into an assertion in <reference osisRef="Ps.82.5">Psa 82:5</reference> of that Psalm. It is not to be translated: will they not have to feel (which ought to be ידעוּ); but also not as Hupfeld renders it: have they not experienced. “Not to know” is intended to be used as absolutely in the signification <hi type="italic">non sapere</hi>, and consequently <hi type="italic">insipientem esse</hi>, as it is in <reference osisRef="Ps.82.5">Psa 82:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.73.22">Psa 73:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.92.7">Psa 92:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.44.18">Isa 44:18</reference>, cf. 9, <reference osisRef="Isa.45.20">Isa 45:20</reference>, and frequently. The perfect is to be judged after the analogy of <hi type="italic">novisse</hi> (Ges. §126, 3), therefore it is to be rendered: have they attained to no knowledge, are they devoid of all knowledge, and therefore like the brutes, yea, according to <reference osisRef="Isa.1.2-Isa.1.3">Isa 1:2-3</reference> even worse than the brutes, all the workers of iniquity? The two clauses which follow are, logically at least, attributive clauses. The subordination of אכלוּ לחם to the participle as a circumstantial clause in the sense of כּאכל לחם is syntactically inadmissible; neither can אכלו לחם, with Hupfeld, be understood of a brutish and secure passing away of life; for, as Olshausen, rightly observes אכל לחם does not signify to feast and carouse, but simply to eat, take a meal. Hengstenberg correctly translates it “who eating my people, eat bread,” i.e., who think that they are not doing anything more sinful, - indeed rather what is justifiable, irreproachable and lawful to them, - than when they are eating bread; cf. the further carrying out of this thought in Mic 3:1-3 (especially Mic 3:3 <hi type="italic">extr</hi>.: “just as in the pot and as flesh within the caldron.”). Instead of לא קראוּ ה Jeremiah says in <reference osisRef="Jer.10.21">Jer 10:21</reference> (cf. however, <reference osisRef="Jer.10.25">Jer 10:25</reference>): לא דרשׁוּ ואת־ה. The meaning is like that in Hos 7:7. They do not pray as it becomes man who is endowed with mind, therefore they are like cattle, and act like beasts of prey.
entries.293049cf583f1d7cb7bd73c6283f12a72bcbc07e: <reference osisRef="Ps.14.5">Psa 14:5</reference> <div eID="gen9156" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9157" type="x-p"/> When Jahve thus bursts forth in scorn His word, which never fails in its working, smites down these brutish men, who are without knowledge and conscience. The local demonstrative שׁם is used as temporal in this passage just as in <reference osisRef="Ps.66.6">Psa 66:6</reference>; Hos 2:17; Zep 1:14; <reference osisRef="Job.23.7">Job 23:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.35.12">Job 35:12</reference>, and is joined with the perfect of certainty, as in <reference osisRef="Job.36.13">Job 36:13</reference>, where it has not so much a temporal as a local sense. It does not mean “there = at a future time,” as pointing into the indefinite future, but “there = then,” when God shall thus speak to them in His anger. Intensity is here given to the verb פּחד by the addition of a substantival object of the same root, just as is frequently the case in the more elevated style, e.g., <reference osisRef="Hab.3.9">Hab 3:9</reference>; and as is done in other cases by the addition of the adverbial infinitive. Then, when God’s long-suffering changes into wrath, terror at His judgement seizes them and they tremble through and through. This judgment of wrath, however, is on the other hand a revelation of love. Jahve avenges and thus delivers those whom He calls עמּי (My people); and who are here called דּור צדּיק, the generation of the righteous, in opposition to the corrupted humanity of the time (<reference osisRef="Ps.12.8">Psa 12:8</reference>), as being conformed to the will of God and held together by a superior spirit to the prevailing spirit of the age. They are so called inasmuch as דּור passes over from the signification <hi type="italic">generatio</hi> to that of <hi type="italic">genus hominum</hi> here and also elsewhere, when it is not merely a temporal, but a moral notion; cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.24.6">Psa 24:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.83.15">Psa 83:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.112.2">Psa 112:2</reference>, where it uniformly denotes the whole of the children of God who are in bondage in the world and longing for deliverance, not Israel collectively in antithesis to the Scythians and the heathen in general (Hitzig).
entries.13d901d23cb37a001dd2254ec804e0c34f0c45a8: <reference osisRef="Ps.14.6">Psa 14:6</reference> <div eID="gen9157" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9158" type="x-p"/> The psalmist himself meets the oppressed full of joyous confidence, by reason of the self-manifestation of God in judgment, of which he is now become so confident and which so fills him with comfort. Instead of the sixth tristich, which we expected, we have another distich. The <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. הבישׁ with a personal object signifies: to put any one to shame, i.e., to bring it about that any one must be ashamed, e.g., <reference osisRef="Ps.44.8">Psa 44:8</reference> (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.53.6">Psa 53:6</reference>, where the accusative of the person has to be supplied), or absolutely: to act shamefully, as in the phrase used in Proverbs, בּן מיבישׁ (a prodigal son). It appears only here with a neuter accusative of the object, not in the signification to defame (Hitz.), - a meaning it never has (not even in <reference osisRef="Prov.13.5">Pro 13:5</reference>, where it is blended with הבאישׁ to make stinking, i.e., a reproach, <reference osisRef="Gen.34.30">Gen 34:30</reference>) - but to confound, put to shame = to frustrate (Hupf.), which is at once the most natural meaning in connection with עצת. But it is not to be rendered: ye put to shame, because..., for to what purpose is this statement with this inapplicable reason in support of it? The <hi type="italic">fut</hi>. תּבישׁוּ is used with a like shade of meaning as in <reference osisRef="Lev.19.17">Lev 19:17</reference>, and the imperative elsewhere; and כּי gives the reason for the tacitly implied clause, or if a line is really lost from the strophe, the lost clause (cf. Isa 8:9.): ye will not accomplish it. עצה is whatsoever the pious man, who as such suffers reproach, plans to do for the glory of his God, or even in accordance with the will of his God. All this the children of the world, who are in possession of worldly power, seek to frustrate; but viewed in the light of the final decision their attempt is futile: Jahve is his refuge, or, literally the place whither he flees to hide himself and finds a hiding or concealment (צל, Arab. <hi type="italic">dall</hi>, סתר, Arab. <hi type="italic">sitr</hi>, Arabic also <hi type="italic">drâ</hi>). מחסּהוּ has an orthophonic <hi type="italic">Dag</hi>., which obviates the necessity for the reading מחסּהוּ (cf. תּעלּים <reference osisRef="Ps.10.1">Psa 10:1</reference>, טעמּו <reference osisRef="Ps.34.1">Psa 34:1</reference>, לאסּר <reference osisRef="Ps.105.22">Psa 105:22</reference>, and similar instances).
entries.06b8a9a691a6934eb6c59002432385173d3ec8a6: <reference osisRef="Ps.14.7">Psa 14:7</reference> <div eID="gen9158" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9159" type="x-p"/> This tristich sounds like a liturgical addition belonging to the time of the Exile, unless one is disposed to assign the whole Psalm to this period on account of it. For elsewhere in a similar connection, as e.g., in <reference osisRef="Ps.126.1-Ps.126.6">Psa 126:1-6</reference>, שׁוּב שׁבוּת means to turn the captivity, or to bring back the captives. שׁוּב has here, - as in <reference osisRef="Ps.126.4">Psa 126:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.2.3">Psa 2:3</reference> (followed by את), cf. <reference osisRef="Ezek.47.7">Eze 47:7</reference>, the <hi type="italic">Kal</hi> being preferred to the <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. השׁיב (<reference osisRef="Jer.32.44">Jer 32:44</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.33.11">Jer 33:11</reference>) in favour of the alliteration with שׁבוּת (from שׁבה to make any one a prisoner of war), - a transitive signification, which Hengstenberg (who interprets it: to turn back, to turn to the captivity, of God’s merciful visitation), vainly hesitates to admit. But <reference osisRef="Isa.66.6">Isa 66:6</reference>, for instance, shows that the exiles also never looked for redemption anywhere but from Zion. Not as though they had thought, that Jahve still dwelt among the ruins of His habitation, which indeed on the contrary was become a ruin because He had forsaken it (as we read in Ezekiel); but the moment of His return to His people is also the moment when He entered again upon the occupation of His sanctuary, and His sanctuary, again appropriated by Jahve even before it was actually reared, is the spot whence issues the kindling of the divine judgment on the enemies of Israel, as well as the spot whence issues the brightness of the reverse side of this judgment, viz., the final deliverance, hence even during the Exile, Jerusalem is the point (the <hi type="italic">kibla</hi>) whither the eye of the praying captive was directed, Dan 6:11. There would therefore be nothing strange if a psalm-writer belonging to the Exile should express his longing for deliverance in these words: who gives = oh that one would give = oh that the salvation of Israel were come out of Zion! But since שׁוב שׁבות also signifies metaphorically to turn misfortune, as in <reference osisRef="Job.42.10">Job 42:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.53">Eze 16:53</reference> (perhaps also in <reference osisRef="Ps.85.2">Psa 85:2</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.14.5">Psa 14:5</reference>), inasmuch as the idea of שׁבוּת has been generalised exactly like the German “<hi type="italic">Elend</hi>,” exile (Old High German <hi type="italic">elilenti</hi> = sojourn in another country, banishment, homelessness), therefore the inscribed לדוד cannot be called in question from this quarter. Even Hitzig renders: “if Jahve would but turn the misfortune of His people,” regarding this Psalm as composed by Jeremiah during the time the Scythians were in the land. If this rendering is possible, and that it is is undeniable, then we retain the inscription לדוד. And we do so the more readily, as Jeremiah’s supposed authorship rests upon a non-recognition of his reproductive character, and the history of the prophet’s times make no allusion to any incursion by the Scythians. <div eID="gen9159" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9160" type="x-p"/> The condition of the true people of God in the time of Absolom was really a שׁבוּת in more than a figurative sense. But we require no such comparison with contemporary history, since in these closing words we have only the gathering up into a brief form of the view which prevails in other parts of the Psalm, viz., that the “righteous generation” in the midst of the world, and even of the so-called Israel, finds itself in a state of oppression, imprisonment, and bondage. If God will turn this condition of His people, who are His people indeed and of a truth, then shall Jacob rejoice and Israel be glad. It is the grateful duty of the redeemed to rejoice. - And how could they do otherwise! The Final Hallelujah  <chapter eID="Ps.14"/> <div eID="gen9160" type="x-p"/>

PSALM 14.
In the beginning the Psalmist describes the wicked contempt of God into which almost the whole people had broken forth. To give the greater weight to his complaint, he represents God himself as uttering it. Afterwards he comforts himself and others with the hope of a remedy, which he assures himself God will very soon provide, although, in the meantime, he groans and feels deep distress at the disorder which he beholds.
“Combien que cependant il gemisse et se sente angoisse du desordre qu’il veoit.” — Fr.
To the chief musician of David.
Psalm 14:1
1. The fool hath said in his heart, There is no God; they have corrupted;
Calvin has here given a literal rendering of the Hebrew words, They have corrupted. Some suppose that themselves is to be understood, as in Exodus 32:7; others, their ways, as in Genesis 6:12, but the meaning which Calvin has attached to the phrase is, They have corrupted or perverted all good order.
, They have done abominable work; there is none that doeth good.
 
Many of the Jews are of opinion that in this psalm there is given forth a prediction concerning the future oppression of their nation: as if David, by the revelation of the Holy Spirit, bewailed the afflicted condition of the Church of God under the tyranny of the Gentiles. They therefore refer what is here spoken to the dispersed condition in which we see them at the present day, as if they were that precious heritage of God which the wild beasts devour. But it is very apparent, that in wishing to cover the disgrace of their nation, they wrest and apply to the Gentiles, without any just ground, what is said concerning the perverse children of Abraham.
“Ce qui est dit de ceux qui, fausses enseignes serenomment enfans d’Abraham vivans autrement qu’il n’appartient.” — Fr. “What is said of those who, according to false marks, call themselves the children of Abraham, while living a different life from what they ought.”
We cannot certainly find a better qualified interpreter than the Apostle Paul, and he applies this psalm expressly to the people who lived under the law, (Romans 3:19.) Besides, although we had not the testimony of this Apostle, the structure of the psalm very clearly shows that David means rather the domestic tyrants and enemies of the faithful than foreign ones; a point which it is very necessary for us to understand. We know that it is a temptation which pains us exceedingly, to see wickedness breaking forth and prevailing in the midst of the Church, the good and the simple unrighteously afflicted, while the wicked cruelly domineer according to their pleasure. This sad spectacle almost completely disheartens us; and, therefore, we have much need to be fortified from the example which David here sets before us: so that, in the midst of the greatest desolations which we behold in the Church, we may comfort ourselves with this assurance, that God will finally deliver her from them. I have no doubt that there is here described the disordered and desolate state of Judea which Saul introduced when he began to rage openly. Then, as if the remembrance of God had been extinguished from the minds of men, all piety had vanished, and with respect to integrity or uprightness among men, there was just as little of it as of godliness.
The fool hath said. As the Hebrew word נבל, nabal, signifies not only a fool, but also a perverse, vile, and contemptible person, it would not have been unsuitable to have translated it so in this place; yet I am content to follow the more generally received interpretation, which is, that all profane persons, who have cast off all fear of God and abandoned themselves to iniquity, are convicted of madness. David does not bring against his enemies the charge of common foolishness, but rather inveighs against the folly and insane hardihood of those whom the world accounts eminent for their wisdom. We commonly see that those who, in the estimation both of themselves and of others, highly excel in sagacity and wisdom, employ their cunning in laying snares, and exercise the ingenuity of their minds in despising and mocking God. It is therefore important for us, in the first place, to know, that however much the world applaud these crafty and scoffing characters, who allow themselves to indulge to any extent in wickedness, yet the Holy Spirit condemns them as being fools; for there is no stupidity more brutish than forgetfulness of God. We ought, however, at the same time, carefully to mark the evidence on which the Psalmist comes to the conclusion that they have cast off all sense of religion, and it is this: that they have overthrown all order, so that they no longer make any distinction between right and wrong, and have no regard for honesty, nor love of humanity. David, therefore, does not speak of the hidden affection of the heart of the wicked, except in so far as they discover themselves by their external actions. The import of his language is, How does it come to pass, that these men indulge themselves in their lusts so boldly and so outrageously, that they pay no regard to righteousness or equity; in short, that they madly rush into every kind of wickedness, if it is not because they have shaken off all sense of religion, and extinguished, as far as they can, all remembrance of God from their minds? When persons retain in their heart any sense of religion, they must necessarily have some modesty, and be in some measure restrained and prevented from entirely disregarding the dictates of their conscience. From this it follows, that when the ungodly allow themselves to follow their own inclinations, so obstinately and audaciously as they are here represented as doing, without any sense of shame, it is an evidence that they have cast off all fear of God.
The Psalmist says that they speak in their heart They may not utter this detestable blasphemy, There is no God, with their mouths; but the unbridled licentiousness of their life loudly and distinctly declares that in their hearts, which are destitute of all godliness, they soothingly sing to themselves this song. Not that they maintain, by drawn out arguments or formal syllogisms, as they term them, that there is no God, (for to render them so much the more inexcusable, God from time to time causes even the most wicked of men to feel secret pangs of conscience, that they may be compelled to acknowledge his majesty and sovereign power;) but whatever right knowledge God instils into them they partly stifle it by their malice against him, and partly corrupt it, until religion in them becomes torpid, and at last dead. They may not plainly deny the existence of a God, but they imagine him to be shut up in heaven, and divested of his righteousness and power; and this is just to fashion an idol in the room of God. As if the time would never come when they will have to appear before him in judgment,
Some critics observe, that as יהוה, Yehovah, the name which denotes the infinite, self-existent essence of God, is not the word here employed, but אלוהס, a name which they regard as referring to God as judge and governor of the world, the meaning of the first verse is not that the fool denies the existence of God, but only his providence and government of the world; that he persuades himself God has no concern about the actions of men, and that there will be no judgment to come; and, therefore, goes on in sin, in the hope of escaping with impunity. — See Poole’s Synopsis Criticorum. The Targum paraphrases the words, “There is no God,” thus, “There is no אלוהס government of God in the earth.”
they endeavor, in all the transactions and concerns of their life, to remove him to the greatest distance, and to efface from their minds all apprehension of his majesty.
“Et abolir de leurs esprits toute apprehension de sa majeste.” — Fr.
And when God is dragged from his throne, and divested of his character as judge, impiety has come to its utmost height; and, therefore, we must conclude that David has most certainly spoken according to truth, in declaring that those who give themselves liberty to commit all manner of wickedness, in the flattering hope of escaping with impunity, deny in their heart that there is a God. As the fifty-third psalm, with the exception of a few words which are altered in it, is just a repetition of this psalm, I will show in the proper places, as we proceed, the difference which there is between the two psalms. David here complains that they have done abominable work; but for the word work, the term there employed is iniquity. It should be observed that David does not speak of one work or of two; but as he had said, that they have perverted or corrupted all lawful order, so now he adds, that they have so polluted their whole life, as to make it abominable, and the proof of this which he adduces is, that they have no regard to uprightness in their dealings with one another, but have forgotten all humanity, and all beneficence towards their fellow-creatures.
Psalm 14:2-3
2. Jehovah looked down from heaven upon the children of men, to see whether there were any that did understand, and seek after God. 3. Every one of them has gone aside, they have altogether become putrid, [or rotten;] there is none that doeth good, not even one,
